The 'first' heaven and earth is the old order marked by sin and death.

readings.reading: Futurists place this after the millennium and the great white throne as the eternal state; dispensationalists (Walvoord) often see a literal renovation by fire (2 Peter 3:10).
Amillennialists (Hoekema, Beale) see the renewed cosmos that immediately follows the single Second Coming and general judgment, the final goal of redemption.

Some partial preterists (Chilton, and in part Gentry) note that the new creation has begun in the new covenant (2 Corinthians 5:17; Isaiah 65 includes death and childbearing), so that 21-22 portrays the church's present glory flowing into its final consummation.

Full preterists identify the new heavens and earth with the new covenant order fully established when the old covenant 'world' (temple and Jerusalem) passed away in AD 70; critics respond that Romans 8 and 2 Peter 3 promise a renewal of the physical creation still awaited, while proponents reply that 'heaven and earth' in prophetic usage can denote a covenant order (Isaiah 51:15-16; 65:17-18).
Historicists (Barnes, Elliott) generally place the new creation after the millennium and final judgment, as the eternal state that ends the prophetic history of the church.

symbols.phrase: And the sea was no more
symbols.jewish: In the Old Testament the sea symbolises chaos and hostile powers: the deep of Genesis 1:2, the sea-monsters Rahab and Leviathan crushed by God (Psalm 74:13-14; Isaiah 27:1; 51:9-10), and the restless wicked (Isaiah 57:20). Daniel's beasts rise from the sea (Daniel 7:2-3). Testament of Moses 10:6 says at the end the sea will retreat into the abyss; Sibylline Oracles 5.447 speaks of the sea drying up.
symbols.cultural: For John on Patmos the sea separated him from the churches; it was also the highway of Rome's commerce (18:17-19) and the direction from which Roman governors arrived in Asia.
symbols.meaning: Not a statement about geography but about the end of everything the sea stood for: chaos, the source of the beast (13:1), death (20:13), separation and the trade of Babylon. It is the first of a series of 'no mores' (21:4; 22:3, 5).

readings.reading: Some literal futurists take it as a physical change in the new earth (no oceans); many futurists also accept its symbolic force.
Idealists and most commentators read it symbolically as the abolition of chaos, evil and separation.

symbols.phrase: The holy city, the new Jerusalem, coming down out of heaven from God
symbols.jewish: Isaiah 52:1 and 60-62 promise a glorified Zion; Ezekiel 40-48 describes a restored temple-city. Tobit 13:16-18; 4 Ezra 7:26 and 10:25-59 (the woman who becomes a city 'not built by human hands'); 2 Baruch 4:2-6 (a pre-existent city shown to Adam, Abraham and Moses); and the Qumran 'New Jerusalem' texts all anticipate a city from God. Galatians 4:26 and Hebrews 12:22 speak of the heavenly Jerusalem.
symbols.cultural: Hellenistic and Roman civic pride centred on city foundations, walls and gates; many cities in Asia Minor claimed divine founders. Rome called itself the eternal city.
symbols.meaning: The city comes 'down', from God: it is gift, not human achievement — the opposite of Babel/Babylon. It is simultaneously a city, a bride (21:2, 9) and a temple (21:22). Many recent commentators follow Gundry in seeing the city primarily as the glorified people of God themselves, while others insist on a real place for real resurrected people (or both).

readings.reading: Dispensationalists (Walvoord, Pentecost) understand a literal city, the eternal home of the redeemed; Pentecost argued that it exists above the earth during the millennium as the dwelling of resurrected saints and then descends to the new earth.
Amillennialists (Beale, Hoekema) see the consummated people of God and new creation pictured as the Edenic temple-city filling the whole earth.

Chilton reads the new Jerusalem as the church, already come down from heaven in the new covenant and replacing apostate earthly Jerusalem after AD 70 (compare Hebrews 12:22), with its fullness yet to come; Gentry likewise stresses its 'already' dimension while affirming future consummation.
Idealists portray the ideal church — God's people as his dwelling — glimpsed now and perfected at the end.
Full preterists view the city as the new covenant community fully established at AD 70, now present as God's dwelling with his people.

symbols.phrase: Prepared as a bride adorned for her husband
keywords: the bride, the wife of the lamb
symbols.jewish: Isaiah 61:10 (a bride adorned with jewels); Isaiah 62:5 (as a bridegroom rejoices over the bride, so God over Zion); Isaiah 49:18 (Zion wearing her children as bridal ornaments). 4 Ezra 10 merges woman and city. Joseph and Aseneth 15 depicts Aseneth's bridal adornment as a City of Refuge.
symbols.cultural: The adornment (kosmeō, the root of 'cosmetic') of a Greco-Roman bride was a public display of honour; the harlot is also adorned (17:4), but with stolen luxury.
symbols.meaning: Completes the marriage announced in 19:7-9. The bride-city is the faithful people of God in covenant intimacy with the Lamb, the antithesis of the harlot-city. The same angel type who showed John the harlot (17:1) now shows the bride (21:9).

symbols.phrase: Behold, the dwelling place of God is with man… They will be His people
symbols.jewish: The Greek skēnē ('tent, tabernacle') and verb skēnoō echo the Hebrew mishkan and the later rabbinic term Shekinah for God's dwelling presence. The covenant formula 'I will put my dwelling among you… and you shall be my people' (Leviticus 26:11-12; Ezekiel 37:27; Jeremiah 31:33; Zechariah 2:10-11; 8:8) is fulfilled. Exodus 25:8 grounds the tabernacle in God's desire to dwell among Israel.
symbols.meaning: The goal of the whole biblical story: God dwelling with his people as in Eden, the tabernacle and the incarnation (John 1:14). Significant manuscripts read 'peoples' (laoi), which would extend Israel's covenant identity to the redeemed of all nations — a textual variant many commentators (Bauckham, Beale) consider original.

symbols.phrase: He will wipe away every tear from their eyes… no more death or mourning or crying or pain
symbols.jewish: Isaiah 25:8 (God swallows up death and wipes tears from all faces); Isaiah 35:10 and 65:19 (no more sound of weeping in Jerusalem). 2 Baruch 73:2-3 and 1 Enoch 25:6 envisage a world without pain or sorrow.
symbols.cultural: Funeral lament and professional mourners were constant features of ancient city life; inscriptions on tombs often expressed hopelessness about death.
symbols.meaning: The tender gesture of God himself, repeating the promise of 7:17. 'The former things have passed away' echoes Isaiah 65:16-17. Death, the last enemy, is gone (20:14).

symbols.phrase: Behold, I make all things new
symbols.jewish: Isaiah 43:18-19 ('Behold, I am doing a new thing') in the context of a new exodus; Isaiah 65:17. 1 Enoch 45:4-5 has God transforming heaven and earth.
symbols.meaning: The first direct speech of God from the throne since 1:8. The present tense ('I am making') has led some to see the renewal as already underway in Christ (2 Corinthians 5:17), consummated at the end. Not 'all new things' but 'all things new' — renewal of the existing creation.

symbols.phrase: It is done! I am the Alpha and the Omega, the Beginning and the End
symbols.jewish: Isaiah 41:4, 44:6 and 48:12: the LORD is the first and the last. A later rabbinic saying (Babylonian Talmud, Shabbat 55a) calls truth (emet: aleph, mem, tav — first, middle and last letters of the Hebrew alphabet) the seal of God; this is late but shows similar alphabet symbolism.
symbols.cultural: Alpha and omega are the first and last letters of the Greek alphabet; letters were also used in Greek magic and numerology. The phrase claims the whole of reality from beginning to end.
symbols.meaning: 'It is done' (gegonan, plural 'they are done') echoes the seventh bowl (16:17) and recalls Jesus' 'It is finished' (John 19:30). God, who began history, now completes it. The same title is used of Jesus in 22:13, a strong statement of his deity.

symbols.phrase: To the thirsty I will give freely from the spring of the water of life
keywords: spring of the water of life
symbols.jewish: Isaiah 55:1 ('come to the waters… without money'); Isaiah 12:3 (wells of salvation); Jeremiah 2:13 (God the fountain of living waters); Psalm 36:9; Zechariah 14:8. 1 Enoch 48:1 describes a fountain of righteousness from which the thirsty drink.
symbols.cultural: Water supply was a constant urban concern in Asia Minor; Laodicea depended on piped water that arrived tepid (3:16), and civic fountains (nymphaea) were monuments of imperial benefaction. Here water is given 'freely' (dōrean), not as patronage.
symbols.meaning: Eternal life is a free gift to all who long for it, anticipating the river of 22:1 and the invitation of 22:17; it also echoes Jesus' offer of living water (John 4:10-14; 7:37-39).

symbols.phrase: The one who overcomes will inherit all things… he will be My son
symbols.jewish: The Davidic covenant promise, 'I will be his father and he shall be my son' (2 Samuel 7:14; Psalm 2:7; 89:26-27), is here extended to every faithful believer. Inheritance of the land (Psalm 37:11; Isaiah 60:21) becomes inheritance of the whole new creation. Jubilees 1:24-25 promises that Israel will be called children of the living God.
symbols.cultural: In Roman law an adopted son received full rights of inheritance — imagery used by Paul (Romans 8:15-17; Galatians 4:5-7).
symbols.meaning: The only place in Revelation where God calls a believer 'my son'. It gathers up all the promises to the overcomers in the seven letters (2:7, 11, 17, 26; 3:5, 12, 21).

symbols.phrase: The cowardly and unbelieving and abominable… their place will be in the lake that burns
symbols.jewish: Vice lists were common in Jewish ethical teaching (Wisdom of Solomon 14:22-27 links idolatry with murder, adultery and deceit). Deuteronomy 20:8 sends the fainthearted home from holy war.
symbols.cultural: Pliny's letter to Trajan (Letters 10.96) describes some who had once confessed Christ but under examination cursed Christ and offered to the emperor's image — the kind of 'cowardice' Revelation warns against.
symbols.meaning: The list heads with 'cowardly' and 'unbelieving' (or 'unfaithful'), aimed at professing believers tempted to compromise under pressure, not only pagan outsiders. The promise and warning together function as an appeal to the churches.

symbols.phrase: He carried me away in the Spirit to a mountain great and high
symbols.jewish: Ezekiel was brought in visions to a very high mountain to see the city-temple (Ezekiel 40:2). Zion is raised above all mountains (Isaiah 2:2; Micah 4:1). Eden was on the mountain of God (Ezekiel 28:13-16). 1 Enoch 24-25 describes a high mountain like a throne beside which stands the tree of life.
symbols.cultural: Greek and Asian cities often had acropolis temples on heights; Pergamum's temples crowned its hill.
symbols.meaning: The vantage point parallels 17:3, where John was carried 'in the Spirit' into a wilderness to see the harlot. The mountain also identifies the city with the cosmic mountain of God — Eden, Sinai and Zion fulfilled.

symbols.phrase: Shining with the glory of God; its radiance like a most precious jewel, like a jasper, clear as crystal
symbols.jewish: The glory of God returns to the temple in Ezekiel 43:2-5 and rises on Zion in Isaiah 60:1-2, 19. The Shekinah glory filled the tabernacle (Exodus 40:34-35).
symbols.meaning: The One on the throne looked like jasper (4:3); now the whole city shares his appearance. The city reflects God himself — the church as the bearer of his glory.

symbols.phrase: A great and high wall with twelve gates inscribed with the names of the twelve tribes of Israel, and twelve angels at the gates
symbols.jewish: Ezekiel 48:30-35: the city's twelve gates, three on each side, bear the names of the tribes. Isaiah 26:1 (salvation as walls) and Isaiah 62:6 (watchmen on Jerusalem's walls). The Qumran New Jerusalem texts and Temple Scroll (11QT 39-41) also assign tribal names to twelve gates.
symbols.cultural: Ancient city walls with monumental gates expressed security and civic identity; city gates were closed and guarded at night.
symbols.meaning: The city fulfils Israel's hope; whether the redeemed community inherits Israel's identity or national Israel keeps a distinct place within it is debated (see the readings). The angels act as gate-guardians or watchmen. John orders the gates east, north, south, west (Ezekiel lists north, east, south, west); proposed significances (e.g., a zodiacal or compass pattern) are speculative.

readings.reading: Dispensationalists see the tribal names as indicating the continuing distinct identity of national Israel alongside the church within the eternal city.
Amillennialists and progressive covenantalists see the tribes and apostles together (21:12-14) as the one people of God of both testaments, Israel's promises fulfilled in Christ's community.

symbols.phrase: Twelve foundations bearing the names of the twelve apostles of the Lamb
symbols.jewish: Isaiah 28:16 (a tested cornerstone in Zion); Isaiah 54:11 (foundations laid with sapphires). The Qumran Community Rule (1QS 8:1-10) describes a council of twelve men as a living foundation and precious cornerstone.
symbols.cultural: Building inscriptions in Greco-Roman cities honoured founders and benefactors on foundations and walls.
symbols.meaning: Twelve tribes on the gates plus twelve apostles on the foundations totals twenty-four, recalling the twenty-four elders (4:4). The church is built on the apostolic foundation (Ephesians 2:20) while entered through the gates of Israel's promises.

symbols.phrase: A golden measuring rod to measure the city and its gates and walls
symbols.jewish: Ezekiel's guide measures the temple with a measuring reed (Ezekiel 40:3-5 onward); Zechariah 2:1-5 shows a man with a measuring line for Jerusalem, which will be a city without walls with God as a wall of fire. The Qumran New Jerusalem texts are largely a record of an angel's measurements.
symbols.cultural: Surveyors laid out Roman colonies and Hellenistic cities with measuring rods; Hippodamian planning prized regular, measured grids.
symbols.meaning: Measuring signifies protection, ownership and the secure establishment of what God has built (compare 11:1-2, where John measured the temple). Gold marks the instrument fit for a holy place.

symbols.phrase: The city lies foursquare… 12,000 stadia in length and width and height
symbols.jewish: The Holy of Holies in Solomon's temple was a perfect cube, twenty cubits each way, overlaid with gold (1 Kings 6:20). Ezekiel's temple and city are square (Ezekiel 45:2; 48:16-20). The Qumran New Jerusalem texts describe a vast rectangular city.
symbols.cultural: Herodotus (1.178) described Babylon as a square city; ancient cities were often measured by circumference. A stadion was about 185-192 metres, so 12,000 stadia is roughly 2,200 km (about 1,400-1,500 miles) — roughly the distance across much of the Roman Mediterranean world.
symbols.meaning: The whole city is a Holy of Holies, the place of God's immediate presence, now as large as the known world. 12,000 is 12 (the people of God) x 1,000 (fullness). Most commentators read the dimensions symbolically; the sheer height has led some literalists to propose a pyramid shape.

readings.reading: Literal futurists (Walvoord, Thomas) take the measurements as the actual dimensions of the future city, allowing that its height may suit glorified life in the new creation.
Idealists and most amillennial commentators (Beale) read the cube as a symbol: the whole people of God become the Holy of Holies, God's presence filling the new creation.
Partial preterists such as Chilton read it as the church as God's temple-city now growing to fill the world, its perfect form showing its completeness and holiness.

symbols.phrase: Its wall 144 cubits, by the human measure the angel was using
symbols.jewish: 144 = 12 x 12, echoing the 144,000 of Israel's tribes (7:4; 14:1). A cubit was about 45-52 cm (forearm length).
symbols.cultural: Roman and Hellenistic city walls were typically a few metres thick and ten to twenty metres high; 144 cubits (about 65-75 metres) would be enormous for a wall, yet tiny against a 2,200-km-high city.
symbols.meaning: Whether thickness or height is meant is unclear. The disproportion suggests symbolism: the wall signals perfect security and the completeness of the people of God. 'Human measure… angel's' perhaps means the measure is understandable to humans though used by an angel.

symbols.phrase: The wall was made of jasper, and the city itself of pure gold, as pure as glass
symbols.jewish: Solomon overlaid the temple and Holy of Holies with pure gold (1 Kings 6:20-22, 30). Tobit 13:16-17 foresees Jerusalem's towers and battlements of pure gold and streets paved with ruby and stones of Ophir.
symbols.cultural: Ancient glass was usually cloudy; perfectly transparent glass was a marvel. Gold was the standard of wealth and was used to gild temples and imperial statues; Nero's 'Golden House' (Domus Aurea) after AD 64 epitomised imperial luxury.
symbols.meaning: Gold transparent as glass is an impossible material, signalling a reality beyond earthly experience — purity and glory without any concealment. The whole city, including its main street (21:21), is a holy sanctuary.

symbols.phrase: The foundations of the city walls were adorned with every kind of precious stone
symbols.jewish: Three backgrounds combine. (1) The high priest's breastpiece of judgment carried twelve stones engraved with the tribes' names (Exodus 28:17-21; 39:10-14); eight of John's twelve names (sardion, topazion, smaragdos, sappheiros, iaspis, amethystos, chrysolithos, bēryllion) appear in the Septuagint list, though in a different order. (2) Isaiah 54:11-12 promises Zion foundations of sapphires, battlements of rubies and gates of jewels. (3) Ezekiel 28:13 lists precious stones covering the figure in Eden. Josephus (Antiquities 3.186; Jewish War 5.234) and Philo (Special Laws 1.87; Life of Moses 2.124) link the breastpiece stones to the twelve months or the signs of the zodiac. Tobit 13:16-17 also has a jewelled Jerusalem.
symbols.cultural: Precious stones were luxury imports from India, Arabia, Egypt and beyond, carved into signets and cameos and worn by the elite; Pliny the Elder's Natural History Book 37 catalogues them. R. H. Charles argued that John's list runs in reverse order of the zodiac signs, as a rejection of astrology; this is widely disputed because ancient lists of zodiacal stones varied.
symbols.meaning: The city is built like the high priest's breastpiece: the whole people of God is the priestly bearer of his presence, every member precious. The Edenic echo makes the city a restored garden-sanctuary. The exact identity of several ancient stone names is uncertain.

readings.reading: Literal futurists expect real gemstones in the future city's foundations, displaying God's glory.
Symbolic readers (Beale, Hendriksen) focus on the priestly and Edenic meanings: the redeemed as a royal priesthood, beautiful and enduring.

symbols.phrase: The first foundation was jasper
symbols.jewish: Jasper (Hebrew yashpheh) is the twelfth stone of the breastpiece in the Hebrew text (Exodus 28:20); the Septuagint places iaspis sixth (Exodus 28:18). It also appears in Ezekiel 28:13.
symbols.cultural: Ancient 'jasper' covered various opaque or translucent stones, often green; Pliny (Natural History 37) describes many colours. John's 'clear as crystal' jasper (21:11) does not match modern opaque jasper, and some suggest rock crystal or even diamond.
symbols.meaning: Jasper is the stone that describes God's own appearance (4:3), the city's radiance (21:11) and its wall (21:18). Placed first, it marks the whole city with God's glory.

symbols.phrase: The second, sapphire
symbols.jewish: Under God's feet at Sinai was a pavement like sapphire (Exodus 24:10); Ezekiel's throne looked like sapphire (Ezekiel 1:26; 10:1); Isaiah 54:11 promises foundations of sapphires — the nearest background for this foundation. The fifth stone of the breastpiece in the Septuagint.
symbols.cultural: Ancient sappheiros was most likely lapis lazuli, a deep blue stone flecked with gold-like pyrite, imported from Afghanistan (Pliny, Natural History 37).
symbols.meaning: The colour of the heavens and of the throne-room floor: the city is founded on the vision of God's throne and fulfils Isaiah's sapphire foundations.

symbols.phrase: The third, chalcedony
symbols.jewish: Chalcedony does not appear in the breastpiece lists or elsewhere in the Bible; its inclusion is one of John's departures from Exodus 28.
symbols.cultural: Named after Chalcedon on the Bosphorus, opposite Byzantium. Its ancient identity is uncertain: possibly a greenish copper-bearing stone Pliny calls the 'Chalcedonian emerald' (Natural History 37), or the milky-blue quartz now called chalcedony.
symbols.meaning: Mostly contributes to the whole picture of varied, brilliant colour; no specific symbolism is clearly established.

symbols.phrase: The fourth, emerald
symbols.jewish: Smaragdos is the third stone of the breastpiece in the Septuagint (Exodus 28:17) and appears in Ezekiel 28:13 and Tobit 13:16 (Jerusalem built with sapphire and emerald). The rainbow round God's throne looked like emerald (Revelation 4:3).
symbols.cultural: Pliny ranks the emerald third among gems and says its green rests the eyes; he reports that Nero watched gladiator fights reflected in an emerald (Natural History 37). Egyptian emerald mines were worked in Roman times.
symbols.meaning: Linked with the rainbow of the throne — the sign of God's covenant faithfulness after judgment (Genesis 9) — now built into the city's foundations.

symbols.phrase: The fifth, sardonyx
symbols.jewish: Not listed by that name in the Septuagint breastpiece list, though onyx stones engraved with the tribes' names sat on the high priest's shoulders (Exodus 28:9-12) and onyx is one of the breastpiece stones (Exodus 28:20).
symbols.cultural: A banded stone of red (sard) and white (onyx) layers, highly prized in Rome for signet rings and cameos (Pliny, Natural History 37); Scipio Africanus is said to have been the first Roman to wear one.
symbols.meaning: Associated with sealing and engraving, it may fit the theme of God's people bearing his name. Its exact identity is reasonably secure but its symbolic value is uncertain.

symbols.phrase: The sixth, carnelian
symbols.jewish: Sardion was the first stone of the breastpiece (Exodus 28:17 Septuagint) and appears in Ezekiel 28:13. The One on the throne looked like jasper and carnelian (Revelation 4:3).
symbols.cultural: The name sardion is traditionally connected with Sardis, one of the seven churches (3:1-6). Reddish carnelian was the commonest stone for Roman engraved signet gems.
symbols.meaning: A blood-red or flesh-coloured stone that, with jasper, describes God's appearance in 4:3; its presence ties the foundations again to the throne vision.

symbols.phrase: The seventh, chrysolite
symbols.jewish: Chrysolithos is the tenth breastpiece stone in the Septuagint (Exodus 28:20, Hebrew tarshish) and appears in Ezekiel 28:13; Ezekiel's wheels (Ezekiel 1:16; 10:9) and Daniel's heavenly man's body (Daniel 10:6) gleam like tarshish.
symbols.cultural: Literally 'gold-stone': a golden-yellow gem, perhaps yellow topaz or citrine; Pliny (37.126) mentions chrysolites from India and Ethiopia. Ancient and modern names do not coincide (modern 'chrysolite' is olivine).
symbols.meaning: Its golden colour matches the gold city; its association with heavenly beings in Ezekiel and Daniel adds to the city's heavenly character.

symbols.phrase: The eighth, beryl
symbols.jewish: Bēryllion is the eleventh breastpiece stone in the Septuagint (Exodus 28:20) and appears in Ezekiel 28:13 Septuagint.
symbols.cultural: A sea-green to blue-green stone; Pliny (Natural History 37) says the best beryls came from India and that lapidaries cut them into hexagonal shapes to enhance their brilliance.
symbols.meaning: Adds sea-green brilliance; any further symbolism is uncertain.

symbols.phrase: The ninth, topaz
symbols.jewish: Topazion is the second breastpiece stone in the Septuagint (Exodus 28:17, Hebrew pitdah); Job 28:19 says the topaz of Cush cannot equal wisdom; Ezekiel 28:13 lists it in Eden; Psalm 119:127 (Septuagint) values God's commands above topaz.
symbols.cultural: Pliny (Natural History 37) says topazos came from an island in the Red Sea, and describes a greenish stone — probably what is now called peridot rather than modern topaz.
symbols.meaning: In Job it represents the most precious earthly wealth, which cannot buy wisdom; in the city it is simply part of the foundation, showing what God gives freely.

symbols.phrase: The tenth, chrysoprase
symbols.jewish: Not in the breastpiece lists or anywhere else in the Bible; another of John's additions.
symbols.cultural: From 'gold' and 'leek': an apple-green or golden-green stone, perhaps the green chalcedony now called chrysoprase; Pliny mentions chrysoprasus from India (Natural History 37).
symbols.meaning: Adds to the variety of colour and the sense of a city built of every precious stone known; no specific symbolism is established.

symbols.phrase: The eleventh, jacinth
symbols.jewish: Hyakinthos does not appear in the Septuagint breastpiece list, but some identify it with the Hebrew leshem, the seventh stone (Exodus 28:19; 'ligure' in the KJV, ligurion in the Septuagint). The colour 'hyacinth' (dark blue-violet) was used for the tabernacle curtains and priestly robes (Exodus 26:1; 28:31 Septuagint).
symbols.cultural: A blue-violet stone named after the hyacinth flower, possibly sapphire or blue zircon; Pliny (Natural History 37) describes it as a violet stone that quickly loses its lustre.
symbols.meaning: The colour of the tabernacle and priestly garments, reinforcing the city's priestly identity; the same colour is used for the demonic cavalry's breastplates in 9:17, now redeemed into holiness.

symbols.phrase: The twelfth, amethyst
symbols.jewish: Amethystos is the ninth breastpiece stone in the Septuagint (Exodus 28:19, Hebrew achlamah).
symbols.cultural: The Greek name means 'not intoxicated'; the stone was popularly believed to protect against drunkenness (Pliny, Natural History 37, reports and doubts such claims). Its purple matched royal dye.
symbols.meaning: A royal purple stone. Some commentators note the contrast with Babylon, who made the nations drunk with the wine of her immorality (14:8; 17:2) — the bride-city is sober and holy — though this is a suggestive rather than certain link.

symbols.phrase: The twelve gates were twelve pearls, each gate a single pearl
symbols.jewish: Isaiah 54:12 promises gates of sparkling jewels. A later rabbinic tradition attributed to Rabbi Yohanan (Babylonian Talmud, Baba Batra 75a; Sanhedrin 100a) says God will set up in Jerusalem's gates enormous pearls and precious stones hollowed out to form gateways — late, but showing the same imaginative tradition.
symbols.cultural: Pearls were the most valuable luxury in Rome (Pliny, Natural History 9, ranks them first among all valuables); Cleopatra is said to have dissolved a priceless pearl in vinegar, and Lollia Paulina paraded jewels worth forty million sesterces. The harlot is adorned with pearls (17:4) and they are among Babylon's cargo (18:12, 16).
symbols.meaning: What Babylon flaunted as status is here the common material of gates open to all. Jesus' parable of the pearl of great price (Matthew 13:45-46) may add that the kingdom is worth everything.

symbols.phrase: I saw no temple in the city, because the Lord God Almighty and the Lamb are its temple
symbols.jewish: Ezekiel's visionary city centres on a rebuilt temple (Ezekiel 40-48), as do the Qumran Temple Scroll and New Jerusalem texts and Tobit 14:5. Jeremiah 3:16-17 foresees a day when the ark will no longer be remembered and Jerusalem itself will be called the throne of the LORD. 1 Enoch 90:28-29 replaces the old house with a new one.
symbols.cultural: Every Greco-Roman city's identity was tied to its temples — Ephesus to Artemis, Pergamum to Zeus, Athena and Augustus. A city with no temple would have been unthinkable.
symbols.meaning: A startling departure from Jewish expectation: the whole city is God's sanctuary (it is a cube like the Holy of Holies), and God's unmediated presence replaces any building. John 2:19-21 and 4:21-24 point the same way.

readings.reading: Dispensationalists distinguish the millennial age, in which they expect Ezekiel's temple to be literally built and used, from the eternal state described here, in which no temple is needed.

Amillennialists (Beale) see Ezekiel 40-48 fulfilled in this vision: the temple promises reach their goal in God and the Lamb dwelling with the people throughout the new creation, not in a future earthly building.
Partial preterists emphasise that after AD 70 no temple-centred worship remains; the church as God's temple (1 Corinthians 3:16; Ephesians 2:21) is the reality the city depicts, perfected at the end.

symbols.phrase: No need of sun or moon… the glory of God illuminates the city, and the Lamb is its lamp; no night there
keywords: no need of sun or moon
symbols.jewish: Isaiah 60:19-20: the sun will no longer be your light, for the LORD will be your everlasting light. Zechariah 14:7: continuous day, with no night. The menorah lamp of the tabernacle burned perpetually before God (Exodus 27:20-21).
symbols.cultural: Sun and moon were worshipped as deities (Helios/Sol, Selene/Luna), and emperors associated themselves with Sol. City gates were shut at nightfall for safety.
symbols.meaning: God's own glory replaces created light; the Lamb is the lamp that holds and spreads it. No night means no danger, no darkness of evil — so the gates never need to be shut.

symbols.phrase: By its light the nations will walk, and into it the kings of the earth will bring their glory
keywords: glory and honor of the nations
symbols.jewish: Isaiah 60:3-11: nations come to Zion's light, kings to the brightness of her dawn, bringing their wealth through gates open day and night. Psalm 72:10-11; Isaiah 2:2-4; Haggai 2:7 (the treasures of all nations shall come). Tobit 13:11 and 14:6 foresee nations turning to God and bringing gifts.
symbols.cultural: Client kings and provinces brought tribute and gifts to Rome; Rome drew the wealth of the nations to itself (18:11-17). In the new city, nations bring their glory freely to God.
symbols.meaning: The 'kings of the earth', elsewhere in Revelation allied with the beast (17:2; 19:19), now bring their glory into the city. Interpreters debate whether this speaks of the redeemed from all nations, the redemption of cultural achievements, or (in a minority view) a wide or universal salvation; Bauckham calls the conversion of the nations a major theme of the book.

readings.reading: Postmillennialists see the fulfilment of the Isaianic hope of converted nations, with Christianised peoples and their cultures offered to God — a goal already being realised in history.
Dispensationalists usually see distinct nations continuing in the eternal state, with Israel and the Gentile nations retaining their identity under God.
Amillennialists such as Hoekema stress that the best of human culture, purified, will be carried into the new earth by the redeemed of every nation.
Idealists read the nations and kings as the redeemed from every people now honouring God, the reversal of the world's allegiance to Babylon.

symbols.phrase: Nothing unclean will ever enter it… only those whose names are written in the Lamb's Book of Life
symbols.jewish: Isaiah 52:1: the uncircumcised and unclean will no longer enter Jerusalem; Isaiah 35:8 (the Way of Holiness); Zechariah 14:21 (no more trader in the house of the LORD). Temple purity laws barred the unclean from the sanctuary (Leviticus 15; Numbers 5:2-3).
symbols.cultural: Herod's temple carried warning inscriptions forbidding Gentiles to pass the barrier on pain of death; two have been found.
symbols.meaning: Holiness, not ethnicity, governs entry: the whole city is a sanctuary, and the only qualification is belonging to the Lamb. The open gates (21:25) and the exclusion of the unclean stand together.

readings.reading: Partial preterists such as Chilton read 21:1-22:5 as a portrait of the new covenant church, the bride that replaced apostate Jerusalem when the old order passed away in AD 70 — already the dwelling of God, healing the nations — while awaiting its final consummation at Christ's return. Gentry and others in the school affirm both this present dimension and a future, physical new creation.

Full preterists see the new heaven and earth and the new Jerusalem as the fully established new covenant world after AD 70, present now for believers; there is no future cosmic renewal. Critics note that this redefines the physical promises of Romans 8 and 2 Peter 3 and stands outside creedal orthodoxy; proponents argue that 'heaven and earth' in prophetic language often means the covenant order.

Historicists generally see chapters 21-22 as the eternal state following the millennium and final judgment, the climax of the church's long history depicted in earlier chapters; some saw partial anticipations in the gospel's spread.

Futurists (Walvoord, Thomas) see the eternal state after the millennium: a literal new earth and a literal city of the stated dimensions and materials. Dispensationalists distinguish the church's heavenly hope from Israel's earthly promises while seeing both united in the city with tribes and apostles.

Idealists (Hendriksen) see the ultimate destiny of the church, also partly realised wherever God dwells among his people now: holiness, beauty, security and unbroken fellowship with God. The city's cube shape (like the Holy of Holies), its gates named for Israel's tribes and foundations named for the apostles, and its point-by-point contrast with Babylon picture the one people of God as the temple filled with his presence.

Eclectic commentators (Osborne, Koester, Bauckham's theological reading) emphasise the symbolic and intertextual richness — Eden, tabernacle, temple and Zion fulfilled — and the city's contrast with Babylon, while affirming a future new creation.

Amillennialists see this as the consummation immediately following the single return of Christ and final judgment: the whole new earth as God's temple, fulfilling Ezekiel 40-48 and Isaiah 60-66 without any intervening earthly kingdom.

Postmillennialists also see the final state after Christ's return but often stress continuity with the gospel's historical victories: the nations' glory brought in is the harvest of the Great Commission.
Dispensational premillennialists see the eternal state after the millennium; some (Pentecost) hold the city already exists above the earth during the millennium as the home of glorified saints.

questions: How does the bride-city of chapter 21 answer, point by point, the harlot-city of chapters 17-18?
What does it mean that the city has no temple? How does that relate to Ezekiel 40-48 and to John 2:19-21?
Is the New Jerusalem a place, a people, or both? What difference does Gundry's 'people as place' reading make?
Why do you think John borrows the high priest's breastpiece for the foundations of the city?
Who are the 'kings of the earth' who bring their glory into the city, given what Revelation says of them earlier?

title: The River and Tree of Life; 'Behold, I Am Coming Soon'
section: The new creation (22:1-5) and the epilogue (22:6-21)
summary: The vision of the New Jerusalem closes with Eden restored: a crystal river of the water of life flows from the throne of God and of the Lamb down the city's main street, and the tree of life stands on either side, bearing twelve crops a year, its leaves for the healing of the nations. The curse is gone, God's servants see his face and bear his name on their foreheads, and they reign forever in his light. The epilogue then authenticates the whole book: the words are faithful and true, the time is near, the prophecy must not be sealed, and Jesus three times declares 'I am coming soon'. John again falls before the angel and is told to worship God; blessings are pronounced on those who keep the prophecy and wash their robes, and those who love falsehood remain outside. Jesus names himself the Root and Offspring of David and the bright Morning Star; the Spirit and the bride invite all who are thirsty; a solemn warning guards the book's words; and the church answers his promise with 'Amen. Come, Lord Jesus!'

outline.heading: The river of the water of life and the tree of life
No more curse: God's servants see his face and reign forever
The words authenticated; 'I am coming soon'; John forbidden to worship the angel
Do not seal the book; the time is near; blessing and exclusion
Jesus' self-testimony; the Spirit and the bride say 'Come'
Warning against adding to or taking from the prophecy
'Yes, I am coming soon.' 'Come, Lord Jesus!' The grace benediction

context:
The opening verses finish the New Jerusalem vision by returning to Genesis 2-3. The Bible's story began with a garden watered by a river, a tree of life, and the presence of God, lost under the curse; it ends with all three restored and expanded into a city. John merges Eden with Ezekiel 47, where a river flows from the temple, deepening as it goes, turning the Dead Sea fresh, lined with trees that bear fruit every month and leaves for healing, and with Zechariah 14:8, where living waters flow out of Jerusalem. Jewish tradition had already linked these: 1 Enoch 24-25 describes the tree of life to be transplanted to the temple for the righteous; 4 Ezra 8:52 promises paradise and the tree of life to the righteous; Testament of Levi 18:10-11 says the messianic priest will open paradise and give the saints to eat of the tree of life. At the Feast of Tabernacles priests poured out water drawn from Siloam at the altar, a rite associated in later tradition with Ezekiel's river and the outpouring of the Spirit — the setting of Jesus' cry in John 7:37-39.

The epilogue (22:6-21) mirrors the prologue (1:1-8): the revelation given through an angel 'to show his servants what must soon take place', a blessing on those who keep its words, the titles Alpha and Omega, and the promise of Christ's coming. It closes in letter form with a grace benediction, as befits a circular letter to the seven churches to be read aloud in worship (1:3, 11). Its warning formula echoes Deuteronomy 4:2 and 12:32 and resembles the curses that ancient authors, treaty-makers and inscriptions placed against anyone altering a text (the Letter of Aristeas 310-311 pronounces a curse on revising the Greek Torah). The cry 'Come, Lord Jesus' renders in Greek the Aramaic prayer marana tha, preserved by Paul (1 Corinthians 16:22) and in the eucharistic prayers of the Didache (10:6). The epilogue's time texts ('soon', 'the time is near', 'I am coming soon') are central to the debate between preterist, historicist, futurist and idealist readings, and the dating of the book (before AD 70 or c. AD 95, disputed) bears directly on how they are read.

symbols.phrase: A river of the water of life, as clear as crystal, flowing from the throne of God and of the Lamb
keywords: river of the water of life
symbols.jewish: A river flowed out of Eden to water the garden (Genesis 2:10-14). Ezekiel 47:1-12 sees water flowing from under the temple threshold, deepening into a river that brings life wherever it goes; Joel 3:18 and Zechariah 14:8 promise living waters from Jerusalem; Psalm 46:4 speaks of a river whose streams make glad the city of God. At Tabernacles, water from the Pool of Siloam was poured at the altar (Mishnah Sukkah 4:9, compiled c. AD 200), a rite later linked to Ezekiel's river.
symbols.cultural: Roman cities prized aqueducts and public fountains; Laodicea's lukewarm, mineral-laden piped water (3:15-16) contrasted with Hierapolis' hot springs and Colossae's cold water. A crystal-clear river flowing through a city was the ideal of urban luxury.
symbols.meaning: Eternal life flows directly from the shared throne of God and the Lamb. John 7:37-39 links the living water with the Spirit, and many see that connection here. The single throne of 'God and the Lamb' is a striking expression of Christ's full divine status.

readings.reading: Chilton and other partial preterists see the river flowing already through the church in the gospel and the Spirit's life, healing the nations through history, with its fullness at the consummation.
Futurists understand a real river in the eternal city (some dispensationalists also expect Ezekiel's river literally in the millennium), with spiritual significance.
Idealists and amillennialists read the river as the life of God given by the Spirit to his people, enjoyed in part now and perfectly in the new creation.

symbols.phrase: Down the middle of the main street of the city
symbols.jewish: Tobit 13:17-18 pictures Jerusalem's streets paved with precious stones and echoing with hallelujahs. Zechariah 8:4-5 envisions old men and children filling the streets of a restored Jerusalem.
symbols.cultural: Hellenistic cities were often organised around a broad colonnaded main street (plateia), the centre of commerce and civic life, such as the Arcadian Way and Curetes Street in Ephesus.
symbols.meaning: The river runs through the public heart of the city, so that the life of God shapes all its common life. The same word is used for the street where the two witnesses' bodies lay in the hostile city (11:8).

symbols.phrase: On either side of the river stood a tree of life, bearing twelve kinds of fruit… a fresh crop each month
symbols.jewish: The tree of life in Eden (Genesis 2:9) was barred after the fall by cherubim and a flaming sword (Genesis 3:22-24). Ezekiel 47:12: fruit trees along the river bearing every month. 1 Enoch 24:4-25:6 describes a fragrant tree to be transplanted to the temple for the righteous after the judgment; 4 Ezra 8:52 and Testament of Levi 18:11 promise access to the tree of life; Psalms of Solomon 14:3 compares the righteous to trees of life. Proverbs uses the tree of life for wisdom (Proverbs 3:18).
symbols.cultural: Colin Hemer proposed that the promise to Ephesus (2:7) plays on the sacred tree-shrine and asylum of Artemis at Ephesus; this connection is suggestive but debated. The Greek word xylon ('wood, tree') was also used by early Christians for the cross (Acts 5:30; 1 Peter 2:24).
symbols.meaning: Fulfils the promise to the overcomer at Ephesus (2:7): what Adam lost is restored. 'Tree' is probably collective (a grove lining both banks). Twelve fruits in twelve months mean perpetual, abundant provision; the number twelve ties the tree to the people of God.

symbols.phrase: The leaves of the tree are for the healing of the nations
symbols.jewish: Ezekiel 47:12: the leaves are for healing. Isaiah 2:2-4 and 60:3 picture nations streaming to Zion; Isaiah 53:5 links healing to the Servant's wounds; Malachi 4:2 speaks of the sun of righteousness rising with healing.
symbols.cultural: Asia Minor was famous for healing cults — the Asclepieion at Pergamum, the medical school at Laodicea with its eye salve (3:18). The true healing of the nations comes from God's tree, not Asclepius.
symbols.meaning: John universalises Ezekiel by adding 'of the nations'. Why healing is needed in a world without pain raises the question whether this describes the present effects of the gospel, the restoration of national life, or simply the fullness of life in the new creation.

readings.reading: Postmillennialists see the healing of the nations as a process already under way through the gospel's progressive triumph in history, flowing into the final state.
Partial preterists (Chilton) read it as the church's present ministry to the nations since the new covenant was fully inaugurated.
Dispensationalists (Walvoord) take the leaves as sustaining the abundant life and health of the nations in the eternal state, not curing disease.
Amillennialists usually see a picture of the complete restoration of humanity from every nation, the curse's effects reversed forever.

symbols.phrase: No longer will there be any curse
keywords: no longer will there be any curse
symbols.jewish: The curse on the ground and on humanity after the fall (Genesis 3:14-19); Zechariah 14:11 promises that Jerusalem will dwell securely and there will be no more 'ban' or curse (herem, devotion to destruction).
symbols.meaning: Everything lost in Genesis 3 is reversed. The phrase also echoes Zechariah: the city will never again be devoted to destruction, unlike Babylon.

symbols.phrase: They will see His face, and His name will be on their foreheads
symbols.jewish: Moses was told no one could see God's face and live (Exodus 33:20); the priestly blessing prays that the LORD make his face shine on his people (Numbers 6:24-26); the psalmists long to behold his face (Psalm 17:15; 27:4; 42:2). The high priest wore a gold plate on his forehead engraved 'Holy to the LORD' (Exodus 28:36-38); Aaron's blessing put God's name on Israel (Numbers 6:27).
symbols.cultural: Slaves and soldiers were sometimes branded or tattooed with the owner's or commander's name; devotees of some cults bore marks of their god. The mark of the beast on forehead or hand (13:16) is the counterfeit.
symbols.meaning: The beatific vision: the highest privilege of Israel's high priest, once a year behind a veil, becomes the permanent privilege of all God's servants. The name on the forehead marks belonging, priestly holiness and transformation into his likeness (1 John 3:2).

symbols.phrase: The Lord God will shine on them, and they will reign forever and ever
symbols.jewish: Daniel 7:18, 27: the saints of the Most High receive the kingdom forever and ever. Numbers 6:25 ('the LORD make his face shine upon you'). Isaiah 60:19-20.
symbols.meaning: The thousand-year reign of 20:4-6 gives way to — or is subsumed into — an everlasting reign. Humanity's original commission to rule creation (Genesis 1:26-28) is restored under God.

symbols.phrase: To show His servants what must soon take place
symbols.jewish: Daniel 2:28-29, 45 (Septuagint/Theodotion) speaks of what must take place 'in the last days' / 'after these things'; Revelation 1:1 and 22:6 reuse the phrase but change it to 'soon' (en tachei), suggesting that what Daniel saw as distant has now drawn near. 'The God of the spirits of the prophets' recalls Numbers 16:22 and 27:16 ('God of the spirits of all flesh') and 1 Enoch's title 'Lord of spirits'.
symbols.meaning: Bracketing the book with 1:1, the verse affirms the trustworthiness and prophetic authority of everything John has seen. The interpretation of 'soon' is a key dividing line between the major approaches.

readings.reading: Partial preterists (Gentry, Chilton) argue that 'soon' and 'near' must be taken at face value for the original readers, so that most of the book's prophecies (the judgment of Jerusalem and Rome's persecuting power) were fulfilled in the first century; the final chapters (20:7-22:5) still reach beyond to the end.

Full preterists (Russell, Preston) hold that 'soon' governs everything in the book, including Christ's coming, the resurrection and the new creation, all fulfilled by AD 70. Critics, including partial preterists, reply that Revelation itself places the final state after a long 'thousand years', and that this view denies the creedal future return; proponents answer that the thousand years is symbolic and fell within that generation.
Futurists explain en tachei as 'quickly/suddenly' once events begin, or as prophetic imminence measured by God's timescale (2 Peter 3:8-9); the events themselves remain largely future.
Historicists understand 'soon' to mean that the chain of fulfilment would begin promptly in John's day and unfold through church history to the end.

Idealists and amillennialists (Beale) read 'soon' as inaugurated eschatology: the last days began with Christ's resurrection, so the end is always near and the book's realities are always pressing upon the church.

symbols.phrase: Behold, I am coming soon
symbols.jewish: Isaiah 40:10 and 62:11: the Lord GOD comes with might, his reward with him. Malachi 3:1 (the Lord will suddenly come to his temple). Habakkuk 2:3 (the vision will surely come and not delay), a text Hebrews 10:37 applies to Christ's coming.
symbols.cultural: The parousia ('arrival') of an emperor or governor to a city was a public event prepared for with ceremony; Christians used the same word for Christ's coming.
symbols.meaning: Spoken three times in the epilogue (22:7, 12, 20), Jesus' promise is the book's final word of hope and warning. Coming 'soon' was also threatened to the churches (2:5, 16; 3:11), where it describes a conditional coming in judgment or help within the readers' lifetimes, which complicates reading every 'coming' as the final Parousia.

readings.reading: Partial preterists distinguish Christ's judgment-comings in history (to the churches, against Jerusalem in AD 70) from his final bodily return; the 'soon' in Revelation refers chiefly to the former, while the book still points to the latter.
Full preterists see one coming of Christ, fulfilled in AD 70 within the lifetime of John's readers.
Futurists see the promise of the personal, bodily Second Coming, imminent in the sense that it could occur at any time and will come suddenly.
Idealists hear both Christ's constant coming to his church in blessing and judgment and the final Parousia toward which all history moves.

symbols.phrase: Blessed is the one who keeps the words of prophecy in this book
keywords: blessed is the one who keeps
symbols.jewish: Blessings on those who keep God's words fill Deuteronomy (e.g. 28:1-14) and the Psalms (Psalm 1; 119:1-2).
symbols.cultural: Revelation was designed to be read aloud in the assembly (1:3); 'keeping' implies obeying and persevering, not merely decoding.
symbols.meaning: The sixth of seven beatitudes, echoing the first (1:3). The purpose of the prophecy is faithful endurance, not speculation.

symbols.phrase: I fell down to worship at the feet of the angel… 'Do not do that!… Worship God!'
symbols.jewish: As in 19:10, the angel's refusal reflects the Jewish conviction, shared with texts like the Ascension of Isaiah 7:21, that angels are fellow servants and must not be worshipped.
symbols.cultural: Angel veneration is attested in Phrygia and the Lycus valley (compare Colossians 2:18).
symbols.meaning: The repetition of 19:10 is deliberate: even an apostle-prophet can be dazzled into misplaced worship. Prophets and all who keep the book are fellow servants with angels; worship belongs to God (and, in Revelation, to the Lamb).

symbols.phrase: Do not seal up the words of prophecy in this book, because the time is near
symbols.jewish: Daniel was told to shut up and seal his words until the time of the end (Daniel 8:26; 12:4, 9), because the fulfilment was far off. Apocalypses often claimed to be sealed writings hidden for a later generation (e.g., 1 Enoch 1:2; 4 Ezra 12:37-38; 14:44-47).
symbols.cultural: Documents were sealed to secure them until an authorised opening; an unsealed letter was meant to be read now.
symbols.meaning: A deliberate reversal of Daniel: what Daniel sealed is now opened because the time has arrived. 'The time is near' repeats 1:3. Preterists regard this contrast as among the strongest arguments for an early fulfilment of much of the book; others read it as marking the arrival of the last days, so it is variously interpreted.

readings.reading: Partial preterists note that Daniel's prophecy, about 400 years from fulfilment, was sealed; Revelation, by contrast, is unsealed, implying fulfilment for its first readers (the AD 60s on an early date).
Futurists reply that 'unsealed' means the message is now to be read and understood, since the last days have begun, not that every event will occur in the first century.
Idealists see the unsealing as the opening of the 'last days' with Christ's resurrection: the book applies to every generation of the church.

symbols.phrase: Let the unrighteous continue to be unrighteous… let the holy continue to be holy
symbols.jewish: Daniel 12:10: many will be purified and made white, but the wicked will continue in wickedness. Ezekiel 3:27 ('he who will hear, let him hear; he who refuses, let him refuse').
symbols.meaning: Not a counsel of indifference but an urgent warning: the time is short, and people are confirming their character. Like the 'he who has ears' formula, it calls for decision while there is time.

symbols.phrase: My reward is with Me, to give to each one according to what he has done
symbols.jewish: Isaiah 40:10 and 62:11 (his reward is with him); Psalm 62:12 and Proverbs 24:12 (God repays each according to his work); Jeremiah 17:10.
symbols.meaning: Christ himself takes on the divine role of judge and rewarder, assigned to God in Isaiah. The note of judgment by works matches 20:12-13.

symbols.phrase: I am the Alpha and the Omega, the First and the Last, the Beginning and the End
symbols.jewish: Isaiah 41:4, 44:6 and 48:12: the LORD, Israel's King and Redeemer, is the first and the last, besides whom there is no God.
symbols.cultural: Greek magical and philosophical texts used alphabet symbolism for cosmic totality; John uses it for the God of Israel.
symbols.meaning: All three titles are combined here and placed on the lips of Jesus. 'Alpha and Omega' and 'Beginning and End' were used of God (1:8; 21:6) and 'First and Last' of Christ (1:17; 2:8); now all belong to Jesus, one of the clearest assertions in the New Testament that he shares the identity of the one God (Bauckham).

symbols.phrase: Blessed are those who wash their robes, so that they may have the right to the tree of life and may enter the city by its gates
symbols.jewish: Israel washed their garments to prepare to meet God at Sinai (Exodus 19:10, 14); priests washed before entering the sanctuary (Exodus 29:4; 40:12); Zechariah 3:3-5 has filthy garments removed from the high priest. Psalm 24:3-4 asks who may ascend the hill of the LORD.
symbols.meaning: The seventh and final beatitude. Robes washed in the blood of the Lamb (7:14) give access to the tree of life — Eden's barrier is lifted. A textual variant (in the Byzantine manuscripts followed by the KJV) reads 'do his commandments' instead of 'wash their robes'; the earlier manuscripts support 'wash their robes'.

symbols.phrase: Outside are the dogs, the sorcerers, the sexually immoral, the murderers, the idolaters
symbols.jewish: 'Dog' was an insult for the impure or the morally degraded; Deuteronomy 23:18 uses it for a male cult prostitute. Dogs were unclean scavengers (1 Kings 21:23-24). Paul turns the term on false teachers (Philippians 3:2). Jesus' saying about not giving holy things to dogs (Matthew 7:6) reflects the same usage.
symbols.cultural: In the Greek world 'dog' was a common insult for the shameless (the Cynic philosophers adopted it). Ancient cities placed cemeteries, refuse and the unclean outside the walls.
symbols.meaning: The vice list (compare 21:8) describes those excluded from the city — not that the wicked live next door in the new creation, but that they have no part in it. Some see the present tense as a call to repentance while there is time.

symbols.phrase: I am the Root and the Offspring of David
keywords: root and the offspring of david
symbols.jewish: Isaiah 11:1, 10: a shoot from the stump of Jesse, the root of Jesse who stands as a banner for the peoples; Jeremiah 23:5 and 33:15 (a righteous Branch for David). Qumran texts expected the 'Branch of David' (4Q174 Florilegium; 4Q285). The Davidic messiah of Psalms of Solomon 17 is the son of David who purges Jerusalem.
symbols.meaning: Jesus is both the source ('root') and the descendant of David — before and after him — combining divine origin and messianic descent (compare Mark 12:35-37). It repeats the title of 5:5 and confirms that Israel's messianic hope is fulfilled in him.

symbols.phrase: The bright Morning Star
symbols.jewish: Balaam's oracle: a star shall come out of Jacob and a sceptre rise out of Israel (Numbers 24:17), read messianically at Qumran (Damascus Document 7:18-21; 4QTestimonia) and later in the name of the revolt leader Simon bar Kosiba, hailed as Bar Kokhba, 'son of the star' (AD 132-135). Isaiah 14:12 mocks the king of Babylon as the 'day star' fallen from heaven. Testament of Levi 18:3 says the messianic priest's star will rise in heaven like a king's.
symbols.cultural: The morning star (Venus, Greek Phōsphoros, Latin Lucifer) heralds the dawn. Venus was the divine ancestress of the Julian emperors, and Roman coinage and propaganda associated emperors with stars (the comet of Julius Caesar was hailed as his deified soul). The promise to Thyatira (2:28) offers the overcomer the morning star.
symbols.meaning: Christ is the dawn-star of the new day that ends the night of the old age; he is the true royal star, not Caesar. The image completes 2:28 and the Davidic theme of Numbers 24.

symbols.phrase: The Spirit and the bride say, 'Come!'… let the one who is thirsty come
symbols.jewish: Isaiah 55:1: come, everyone who thirsts, buy without money. Wisdom's invitation in Proverbs 9:1-6 and Sirach 24:19-21 calls the hungry to eat and drink.
symbols.cultural: In the liturgical setting where Revelation was read aloud, this verse may have formed a call-and-response, possibly leading into the Lord's Supper.
symbols.meaning: The first two 'Comes' are probably addressed to Christ (answering 'I am coming soon'); the third is an invitation to the thirsty to come and take the water of life freely. The church, empowered by the Spirit, prays for Christ's coming and invites the world to him in the same breath.

symbols.phrase: If anyone adds to them… if anyone takes away from the words of this book
symbols.jewish: Deuteronomy 4:2 and 12:32: do not add to or subtract from the commandments; Deuteronomy 29:20 calls down every curse written in the book on the covenant breaker. The Letter of Aristeas 310-311 records a curse on anyone revising the Greek translation of the Law; 1 Enoch 104:10-11 warns against altering the words.
symbols.cultural: Ancient treaties, wills, inscriptions and books often ended with curse formulas against tampering; copyists' changes were a known problem (Irenaeus, Against Heresies 5.30.1, complains about manuscripts altering 666 to 616).
symbols.meaning: The warning guards the prophecy as covenant word: distorting it through falsification or by twisting its message to suit compromise invites its plagues or loses its blessings. It is addressed to 'everyone who hears', i.e. the churches, and is a canonical seal on Revelation rather than on the whole Bible, though many have applied it more widely.

symbols.phrase: 'Yes, I am coming soon.' Amen. Come, Lord Jesus!
symbols.jewish: The Greek prayer translates the Aramaic marana tha ('Our Lord, come!'), preserved untranslated in 1 Corinthians 16:22 and in the eucharistic prayer of the Didache (10:6). Its survival in Aramaic shows that the earliest Jewish-Christian communities in Palestine addressed Jesus as 'Lord' (mar) in prayer and longed for his coming.
symbols.cultural: Cities prepared for the parousia ('arrival') of an emperor with prayers, processions and acclamations; Christians reserved their longing for the coming of their true Lord.
symbols.meaning: Christ's last promise and the church's response form the final dialogue of the Bible. 'Amen' affirms the promise; 'Come, Lord Jesus' is the prayer of a church that wants his coming, not merely predicts it.

readings.reading: Partial preterists hear an expectation of Christ's imminent coming in judgment on the persecutors (fulfilled in the first century) that still models the church's prayer for his final return.

Full preterists see this prayer as answered in AD 70; critics respond that the church has always prayed it as a future hope, as in the Lord's Supper 'until he comes' (1 Corinthians 11:26); proponents reply that Paul wrote those words to a generation that expected the coming within its lifetime.
Futurists see the church's prayer for the personal, bodily return of Christ, which remains imminent.
Idealists see the perpetual longing of the church in every age for Christ's coming, experienced partially in worship and fully at the end.
Historicists hear the prayer of a church that has lived through the long history the book foretells, still awaiting its final chapter.

symbols.phrase: The grace of the Lord Jesus be with all the saints. Amen
symbols.jewish: Jewish letters and prayers commonly closed with blessings of peace and an Amen (compare Numbers 6:24-26).
symbols.cultural: Revelation is framed as a letter (1:4-5) to the seven churches; Paul's letters end with almost identical grace benedictions (e.g. 1 Corinthians 16:23; Galatians 6:18).
symbols.meaning: A book full of judgment ends with grace. The epistolary close reminds readers that Revelation was sent to real congregations, to be read and obeyed in worship.

readings.reading: Partial preterists (Gentry, Chilton, Mathison) see 22:1-5 as the consummation of the new covenant order begun in the first century and stress that the epilogue's time texts ('soon', 'near', 'do not seal') show that most of the book's judgments fell within its first readers' lifetime, while the final coming, resurrection and new creation remain future.

Full preterists (Russell, King, Preston) apply the epilogue's 'soon' to the entire book, so that Christ's coming, the new creation and the river of life became realities in AD 70. Critics, including partial preterists, regard this as outside the historic creeds because it denies a future bodily return and resurrection; proponents reply that the time texts allow no other conclusion.

Historicists read the epilogue as confirming a prophecy that began to be fulfilled 'soon' in John's day and continues through church history to the final consummation; 22:1-5 describes the eternal state.

Futurists see 22:1-5 as the eternal state after the millennium and read the time texts as stressing the certainty, suddenness and imminence of Christ's still-future return. They note that the unsealing of 22:10 reverses Daniel 12:4 because the last days began with Christ (Hebrews 1:2), not because every event must fall within one generation, and that the promised reward (22:12) belongs to the personal return the church has always awaited.

Idealists see the river and tree as God's life given to his people now in part and fully at the end, and the epilogue's urgency as applying to every generation in the inaugurated last days. Hendriksen and Beale stress that the closing blessings and warnings are addressed to 'everyone who hears' (22:18), so the book's call to faithful endurance binds every generation equally.
Eclectic commentators (Osborne, Keener) affirm both the first-century urgency of the epilogue for the seven churches and a still-future consummation, reading 'soon' as prophetic imminence.
Amillennialists see Eden restored in the new creation immediately after the single return of Christ, with the time texts expressing the already-not-yet of the last days.
Postmillennialists emphasise the healing of the nations and the river flowing outward as the long-term fruit of the gospel, consummated at Christ's return.

Dispensational premillennialists see the eternal state after the literal millennium and take the time texts as describing the sudden and imminent character of the coming, consistent with a pretribulational rapture that could occur at any moment.
